Theorem: Let $p$ be any prime number. The set of $p$-adic numbers $\mathbb{Q}_p$ is an uncountable set.

Proof:
Consider the set of $p$-adic integers, denoted by $\mathbb{Z}_p$. The set $\mathbb{Z}_p$ is a subset of the $p$-adic numbers $\mathbb{Q}_p$ (specifically, it is the valuation ring of $\mathbb{Q}_p$, consisting of all elements $x \in \mathbb{Q}_p$ with $p$-adic norm $|x|_p \le 1$).

Every $p$-adic integer $x \in \mathbb{Z}_p$ can be represented uniquely by a formal power series in $p$:
$x = \sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n p^n$
where each coefficient (or digit) $a_n$ is an integer such that $0 \le a_n < p$. Because this representation is strictly unique for every $p$-adic integer, there is a bijection between $\mathbb{Z}_p$ and the set of all infinite sequences $(a_0, a_1, a_2, \ldots)$ with terms in $\{0, 1, \ldots, p-1\}$.

We use Cantor's diagonal argument to prove that $\mathbb{Z}_p$ is uncountable.
Suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that $\mathbb{Z}_p$ is countable. Then its elements can be listed in an infinite sequence $x^{(0)}, x^{(1)}, x^{(2)}, \ldots$.
Each $x^{(i)}$ in this list has a unique $p$-adic expansion:
$x^{(i)} = \sum_{n=0}^\infty a_{i,n} p^n$
where $a_{i,n} \in \{0, 1, \ldots, p-1\}$.

We can construct a new $p$-adic integer $y$ by defining its $p$-adic expansion as:
$y = \sum_{n=0}^\infty b_n p^n$
where the digits $b_n$ are chosen as follows:
$b_n = \begin{cases} 
1 & \text{if } a_{n,n} = 0 \\ 
0 & \text{if } a_{n,n} \ne 0 
\end{cases}$

Since $p$ is a prime, we have $p \ge 2$, meaning both $0$ and $1$ are valid digits in $\{0, 1, \ldots, p-1\}$. Thus, each $b_n$ is a valid digit, which implies that $y$ is a well-defined $p$-adic integer, and therefore $y \in \mathbb{Z}_p$.

However, by our construction, the $n$-th digit of $y$ ($b_n$) is strictly different from the $n$-th digit of $x^{(n)}$ ($a_{n,n}$) for every $n \ge 0$. Consequently, $y$ cannot be equal to $x^{(n)}$ for any $n \ge 0$. 

This means that $y$ is not in our enumerated list $x^{(0)}, x^{(1)}, x^{(2)}, \ldots$, which contradicts the assumption that the list contains all elements of $\mathbb{Z}_p$. 
Thus, our assumption that $\mathbb{Z}_p$ is countable must be false, proving that $\mathbb{Z}_p$ is an uncountable set.

Because $\mathbb{Z}_p$ is a subset of $\mathbb{Q}_p$, and any set that has an uncountable subset must itself be uncountable, we conclude that the set of $p$-adic numbers $\mathbb{Q}_p$ is uncountable. $\blacksquare$
